objectives: This systematic review aimed to consolidate observational evidence on the association between spirochaetal infection and neurodegenerative disease. A secondary objective was to identify gaps in the current literature and highlight areas for future research into the pathogenic mechanisms of neurotropic spirochaetes, to inform evidence-based approaches to diagnosis and treatment.
inclusion_criteria: Studies were eligible if they were published, peer-reviewed original articles; human studies in adult populations; reported diagnosis or seropositivity of spirochaetal infection to a clinically acceptable standard; assessed cognitive function, impairment, decline, or diagnoses such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or other dementias using standardized methods; used an observational design (cross-sectional, cohort, or case-control; prospective or retrospective); and were written in English with full-text availability. Clinically acceptable infection diagnosis was defined as validated laboratory methods appropriate to each organism: for T. pallidum, treponemal and non-treponemal tests used according to clinical guidelines; for B. burgdorferi, validated two-tier or modified two-tier serological testing or CSF antibody index; and for Leptospira spp., ELISA, microscopic agglutination test, or PCR-based confirmation. Cognitive impairment had to be assessed with validated tools such as MMSE, MoCA, or Clinical Dementia Rating, or by formal diagnostic criteria such as DSM-5, ICD-11, or NINCDS-ADRDA.
